result.abstractText: Single applications of silicon (Si) and salicylic acid (SA) can alleviate plant stress. However, the effects of their combined application on dry-cultivated rice and the differences between varieties remain unclear. A preliminary laboratory experiment established the optimal silicon fertilizer application rate at 45 kg ha<sup>-1</sup>. Subsequently, a preliminary experiment conducted in 2022 determined the optimal SA concentration at 1.0 mM. Based on these findings, four treatments were set up in 2023: control (CK), single application of Si (T1), single application of SA (T2), and Si + SA (T3). The results indicated that the combined application of Si and SA significantly enhanced both the grain yield and photosynthetic capacity of dry-cultivated rice. Under the T3 treatment, grain yield increased by 80.7% and 77.3% in cultivars SJ18 and HK88, respectively, compared with the CK. This yield improvement was primarily attributable to increases in two key yield components: the number of effective panicles (up by 17.6% and 29.3%, respectively) and the number of grains per panicle (up by 26.9% and 22.6%, respectively). The responses of the agronomic traits to the treatment were consistent with the yield trends. Physiologically, the combined application of Si + SA enhanced the photosynthetic capacity of the photosystem II (PSIl) system by improving chlorophyll fluorescence parameters, increasing antioxidant enzyme activities, and enhancing soluble sugar, soluble protein content, endogenous SA, and Si contents. The responses of different varieties to the combined application of Si + SA differed significantly. 10 days after spraying, the soluble sugar and protein content of HK88 increased by 36.1% and 22.7%, respectively, compared with CK, which were numerically greater than the corresponding increases observed in SJ18 (10.7% and 17.4%, respectively). This finding suggests that drought-resistant varieties may require greater accumulation of osmotic adjustment substances to alleviate drought stress. Therefore, the combined application of SA and Si is closely associated with increased levels of osmotic adjustment substances and endogenous SA and Si, as well as enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities. These coordinated physiological responses contribute to enhanced photosynthetic capacity of the PSII system, ultimately improving drought tolerance, dry matter accumulation, and grain yield in dry-cultivated rice. These relationships are further supported by significant positive correlations observed in our structural equation modeling analysis. This approach provides a new and effective way of alleviating drought stress and increasing the yield of dry-cultivated rice.

result.abstractText: Root-associated microbiomes contribute to plant nutrition, defense and stress tolerance, but their variable responses across hosts and environments limit the predictability of microbiome-based interventions. This review examines plant physiological regulation of root microbiome assembly and feedback under environmental stress. Evidence from plant and microbial genetics, defined-metabolite assays, synthetic communities and physiological analyses links changes in carbon allocation, nutrient status, hydraulics, redox balance and hormone-immune signaling to root-derived outputs and microbial responses. These outputs influence microbial sensing and resource use, while host immune and metabolic conditions help regulate colonization and persistence. Flavonoid-NodD signaling, strigolactone-induced mycorrhizal fungal responses and coumarin-mediated selection illustrate comparatively well-resolved transitions; the roles of stress-associated purines, nucleotides and compatible solutes remain more context dependent. However, microbial enrichment and metabolite associations alone do not establish plant-controlled recruitment or benefit. Stronger evidence connects plant regulation, microbial response mechanisms and physiological outcomes through causal perturbations. Microbial activity can modify host physiology, although evidence that the altered host state subsequently redirects community assembly remains limited. We integrate these illustrative findings into a framework linking physiological regulation, root outputs, microbial responses, establishment and feedback. This synthesis identifies testable connections for improving microbiome interventions under stress. Translation requires attention to plant carbon and immune costs, competition within resident communities, and validation across host genotypes and environments.

result.abstractText: Understanding plant water uptakes in alpine wetlands are pivotal for sustaining water conservation and maintaining ecological safety of the lower reaches under continuous wetland degradation. However, the physiological integration, a unique process in clonal plants, of water uptake and morphological adaptation in these ecosystems remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, the water uptake sources, functional traits, and biomass allocation of Potentilla anserina were examined along a riverbank distance gradient in the Zoige Alpine Wetland under spacer-severing and intact-spacer treatments. The results indicated that P. anserina predominantly utilized shallow soil water according to the isotope indicators, while the water-source use exhibited pronounced seasonal plasticity, with the strongest sensitivity to soil moisture in autumn when root gradients were well developed. The xylem water isotope values were significantly lower in intact ramets than in severed ones, and the physiological integration significantly promoted the deep-water uptake through clonal networks. Compared with the intact groups, the severed ramets displayed lower specific leaf area (SLA) and leaf water content (LWC), but higher leaf dry matter content (LDMC), water-use efficiency (WUE), sensitivity of water uptake to soil moisture, and greater biomass allocation to belowground organs. These trait adjustments indicate a shift from an acquisitive strategy to a conservative strategy along the leaf economic spectrum. However, root traits did not fully correspond to the leaf economic spectrum, suggesting a multidimensional nature of root function. Overall, these findings emphasize the unignorable impacts of spacers in plant water acquisition and ecological adaptation, providing novel insights into vegetation restoration and water management in alpine wetlands.
